sector: Building Materials / Glass Processing & Glazing (NZ & Australia construction supply chain)
overview: Metro Performance Glass (Metroglass) is Australasia's leading processor of flat glass, supplying double-glazed insulated glass units (IGUs) and related processed glass products for the residential and commercial construction and renovation markets. The Group operates two manufacturing plants in New Zealand (Auckland/Highbrook and Christchurch) with a nationwide glazing/branch distribution network, and a wholly-owned Australian subsidiary, Australian Glass Group (AGG), which processes and now also imports IGUs from three sites in Melbourne, Sydney and Hobart. FY26 (year to 31 March 2026) group revenue was $208.2m (NZ $130.4m, AGG A$77.8m), down from $213.9m in FY25, reflecting a prolonged construction-sector downturn in both countries.

business_model.summary: Metro converts float glass into value-added processed and insulated glass products (toughened, laminated, low-E, double glazing) sold to window/door fabricators, builders and, in New Zealand, direct to trade/retail through its own glazing branch network. Revenue is transactional/project-based (tied to construction activity and building consents) rather than recurring/subscription, so it moves with residential and commercial building cycles with a lag. Roughly 63% of FY26 revenue was New Zealand, 37% Australia (AGG).

revenue_streams.name: New Zealand processed/IGU glass and glazing services
revenue_streams.trend: declining (residential pricing pressure, North Island weakest)

revenue_streams.name: Australia Glass Group (AGG) - Victoria, NSW, Tasmania

business_model.customer_type: B2B - window and door fabricators, builders/developers, commercial glaziers, with some direct trade/retail glazing services in NZ
business_model.geographic_mix: New Zealand ~63% (Auckland/Highbrook and Christchurch plants), Australia (AGG) ~37% (Melbourne, Sydney, Hobart; south-eastern Australia climate zones favouring insulated glass)

main_competitors: Viridian Glass (Australasia's largest glass products producer)
Oceania Glass (Australia, closed during FY26, shifting AGG to an import model)
competitive_position.market_position: Largest dedicated glass processor in New Zealand and a top-tier processor/importer in south-eastern Australia via AGG, but operating in a structurally oversupplied NZ market amid a subdued building cycle

moat_factors.description: Two large NZ plants plus AGG's three Australian sites give processing scale and a national distribution/glazing network competitors of sub-scale cannot easily replicate

Long operating history (30+ years); FY26 DIFOT (delivery-in-full-on-time) improved sharply to 93.4% (AKL) and 98.8% (CHC), and management notes conversations with customers are shifting from price to quality/service

NZ Building Code and Australian NatHERS energy-efficiency changes increasingly mandate double glazing and higher-performance IGUs, structurally growing addressable demand for Metro's higher-margin product mix
Nationwide branch/glazing network in NZ captures installation value beyond pure glass processing

weaknesses: New Zealand glass processing market is oversupplied relative to current building activity, per Commerce Commission's own findings during the Viridian review, keeping pricing under structural pressure
High fixed-cost manufacturing base with volume-led legacy model was a driver of past losses; still transitioning to a more disciplined, margin-led model
No pricing power in a commoditised, price-competitive segment of the market despite service improvements
AGG historically loss-making/turnaround-dependent; closure of major Australian supplier Oceania Glass forced a costly (~A$1m incremental cost) shift to an import model
Small-cap, thinly-traded NZX stock with concentrated (51%) ownership by a single strategic investor (Amari/Metro Glass Investment), limiting free float and float-based liquidity

growth_drivers: Structural build-out of double glazing/insulated glass demand driven by tightening energy-efficiency codes (NZ Building Code changes; Australia's NatHERS updates embedded in NSW/Victoria) supporting higher-value product mix
Australian Federal Government's stated target of 1.2 million new homes over five years supporting medium-term AGG volume recovery once the housing cycle turns
Growing share of higher-performing Low-E glass, custom laminated safety glass, digital printing, frameless systems and retrofit double glazing - all higher-margin than commodity float processing

FY26 cost-out program ($4m of NZ operating cost reduction, headcount and plant/logistics restructuring) expected to deliver a full-year benefit in FY27, creating operating leverage as volumes stabilise or recover
Balance-sheet reset (September 2025 equity raise, new 3-year banking facility to Sept 2028) removes going-concern doubt and frees management to focus on commercial execution rather than survival

Potential further consolidation in a currently oversupplied NZ market (Viridian's failed takeover shows ongoing industry consolidation interest) could rationalise capacity and support pricing over time

business.description: FY26 revenue fell 2.7% with particular weakness in North Island residential (down to $76.5m) and Victoria, Australia; management explicitly is 'not building any substantive market growth' into FY27 guidance
NZ glass processing capacity structurally exceeds current demand, per Commerce Commission findings, keeping pricing competitive and margins compressed
Closure of Oceania Glass forced AGG to shift to a full import model, adding ~A$1m of incremental costs in FY26 with further transition risk

New CEO (Simon Bennett, appointed MD Sept 2025), new CFO, and multiple country-manager changes (NZ, Australia, Victoria/Tasmania/NSW) during FY26 create key-person and integration risk during a fragile recovery

financial.description: Despite reducing net debt to $27.0m (from $60.5m) via the Sept-2025 raise and refinancing, the group remains loss-making at the statutory level (FY26 net loss $0.9m) and covenant headroom depends on the FY27 earnings recovery materialising
Company has already needed two recapitalisations in recent years (2019 debt reduction priority, Sept-2025 $23.9m raise); any renewed stress could require further equity issuance
AGG's Australian-dollar earnings translate into NZD reporting; FX moved favourably in FY26 (translation gain) but is a two-way risk
IFRS16 lease liabilities ($69.5m total, current + non-current) are larger than bank interest-bearing debt ($35.2m), so reported net debt understates total fixed financing-type obligations

regulatory.description: The Commerce Commission's scrutiny of the Viridian bid (unresolved competition concerns before withdrawal) signals regulators view the NZ glass market as concentrated, which could constrain future consolidation/M&A upside for Metro

regulatory.risk: Building code and energy-efficiency regulatory change
regulatory.description: Generally a tailwind (more double glazing mandated) but implementation timing/scope changes create demand-forecast uncertainty

macro.risk: NZ and Australian residential construction cyclicality
macro.description: Revenue is directly linked to building consents and renovation activity; NZ consents growth has been volatile in 2026 (double-digit y/y gains early in the year, momentum slowing mid-year) and architects expect a net contraction in the pipeline
Higher-for-longer interest rates in NZ/Australia depress new housing starts and renovation spend, the primary demand driver for Metro's products, and also raise Metro's own refinancing cost
Wages, fuel and imported float glass/component costs remain inflationary pressures management is trying to offset with efficiency gains

macro_factors.industry_outlook: NZ residential building consents showed strong y/y growth into mid-2026 (issued dwellings up ~16-19% y/y through April/May 2026) but momentum weakened sharply in June (consents -4% m/m) and forward-looking surveys point to a net contraction in the architects' pipeline over the coming year; the Australian market (particularly Victoria, AGG's core) remains subdued near-term but has longer-term structural support from a 1.2 million new homes federal target
macro_factors.cyclicality: High - revenue and volumes track residential and commercial construction cycles in both New Zealand and Australia with typical lags
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: High indirect sensitivity via construction/housing activity; moderate direct sensitivity via Metro's own borrowing costs (finance expense fell from $11.4m to $8.7m in FY26 on debt paydown)
key_input_costs: Imported IGU components from new Australian suppliers post-Oceania Glass closure

recent_developments.event: FY26 (audited) results released: revenue $208.2m (-2.7%), EBITDA before significant items $18.2m (up from $16.9m), EBIT before significant items $0.9m (from -$0.6m loss), net loss $0.9m (narrowed from $13.5m), net debt cut to $27.0m from $60.5m, operating cash flow up to $15.7m from $2.1m; going-concern uncertainty removed by auditors

Amari Metals Australia transferred its 51% Metro Performance Glass shareholding to affiliate Metro Glass Investment (MGI) Pty Ltd in an internal group restructure - control unchanged, same ultimate ownership

Viridian NZ BidCo (backed by Crescent Capital Partners) formally withdrew its Commerce Commission clearance application to acquire up to 100% of Metro Performance Glass, ending a long-running takeover attempt amid unresolved Commission competition concerns

Recapitalisation completed: $23.9m equity raise (1.6-for-1 pro-rata rights offer raising $8.9m plus up to $15m Amari Metals Australia placement), new 3-year banking facility through September 2028 negotiated with lending syndicate; proceeds primarily used to repay debt

Simon Bennett appointed Managing Director (previously a director from Dec-2023); new Chair Shawn Beck and new non-independent director Stephen Robertson (Amari-affiliated) joined the Board reflecting Amari's cornerstone stake
Special General Meeting - shareholders approved all recapitalisation resolutions (equity raise, Amari placement, board changes) with strong support

Oceania Glass (a major Australian glass supplier) closed, forcing AGG to transition to a full import model for glass supply, adding roughly A$1m of incremental costs but opening new supplier relationships
H1 FY26 (half year to 30 Sept 2025) swung to a $2.9m profit from a $5.0m loss in H1 FY25, driven by a $8.6m significant-item gain (debt extinguishment) alongside underlying trading improvement

items.target: Improvement expected across NZ and Australia
items.notes: Management expects 'stronger cash flow, lower debt, and higher revenue and profitability in both Australia and New Zealand,' driven by disciplined revenue growth (targeted price increases, volume growth in priority regions) and margin improvement; no specific numeric guidance provided given ongoing macro uncertainty

items.target: Meaningful improvement, return to positive pre-IFRS16 earnings at group level
items.notes: Full-year benefit of FY26 headcount reductions, plant/logistics restructuring and AGG import-model stabilisation expected to flow through; one-off FY26 costs (~$1m AGG import transition) not expected to repeat
Management explicitly stated it is 'not building any substantive market growth' into the forward outlook; guidance is self-help/cost-driven, not volume-recovery-driven
Company stated there remains 'enough uncertainty' that it is not providing specific performance guidance for FY27 at this stage

guidance.management_commentary: MD Simon Bennett: FY26 was about stabilising the business and resetting the capital structure (removal of going-concern note); FY27 is about converting operational improvements (record DIFOT, quality metrics, $4m of realised cost cuts) into revenue growth and margin expansion. Management is monitoring geopolitical/Iran-related supply risk with contingency plans, and remains cautious on both NZ and Australian construction end-markets while expressing confidence in the company's lower cost base and improved product/service differentiation versus a year ago.

bull_case: Balance sheet has been fundamentally reset - net debt cut from $60.5m to $27.0m, going-concern doubt removed, and a new 3-year banking facility to Sept-2028 provides runway to execute the turnaround without financing distraction

FY26 cost-out program ($4m of NZ opex reduction, AGG restructuring) has largely been actioned but its full-year P&L benefit will only show up in FY27, creating built-in operating leverage even without a market recovery

Failed Viridian takeover and continuing industry oversupply keep consolidation optionality alive; a strategic 51% cornerstone shareholder (Amari/MGI) with board representation signals long-term committed capital rather than a distressed overhang

Structural regulatory tailwind toward higher-performance double glazing/IGUs in both NZ (Building Code) and Australia (NatHERS) should lift Metro's product mix and margins over a multi-year horizon independent of the building cycle's amplitude
Operational KPIs (DIFOT, quality/rework rates) improved sharply in FY26, evidencing a genuine service-led turnaround that could support premium pricing and share gains as the market stabilises
bear_case: Company remains statutorily loss-making (FY26 net loss $0.9m) in a construction downturn that management itself says shows no signs of a substantive recovery, with NZ consent momentum already slowing mid-2026 and architects forecasting a further pipeline contraction

NZ glass processing market is structurally oversupplied (a finding that surfaced during Commerce Commission's review of the Viridian bid), limiting Metro's ability to raise prices even as costs (wages, fuel, imports) inflate

Small-cap, thinly-traded NZX stock with 51% held by a single strategic investor (Amari/MGI) - limited free float constrains liquidity and gives one shareholder effective control over strategic decisions and future capital raises

Track record of value destruction: multiple recapitalisations (2019 balance-sheet stress, Sept-2025 $23.9m dilutive raise) and a history of Australian operational missteps (AGG impairments, Oceania Glass supply disruption) raise execution-risk questions for the current leadership team, much of which is newly appointed

No specific FY27 numeric guidance was provided, and management's own language ('enough uncertainty') suggests limited visibility into whether the self-help cost program will be sufficient to offset a still-weak top line
